opus-5.5.text:
I think a useful way to frame it is this: language models are extremely good at problems where the world has already been compressed for you. Language is a human invention. It's discrete, symbolic, and highly abstracted, and every sentence on the internet is already the output of a human brain that has perceived the world, filtered it, and turned it into concepts. So when an LLM learns from text, it's learning from a pre-digested representation of reality. That's why it can do reasoning, coding, math, and knowledge retrieval so well. Those are things that live natively in the symbolic space.

Vision is fundamentally different. The visual signal is raw. It's continuous, high-dimensional, extremely redundant, and nobody has done the abstraction for you. A pixel doesn't mean anything by itself. So the core problem in vision isn't just "predict the next token" but how to go from this messy, physical sensory stream to a representation that captures structure: objects, geometry, physics, causality, how things move and interact over time.

So the distinction I often make is that LLMs solve the problems of the *mind as it expresses itself*, while vision has to solve the problems of *grounding*, of understanding the world as it actually is, not as we describe it. There are many things we never write down because they're too obvious to us: how a cup falls off a table, how light bounces around a room, how far you need to reach to grab something. Animals with no language at all understand these things perfectly. That kind of intelligence doesn't come from text, and you can't get it just by scaling text.

That's also why I'm a bit cautious about the view that vision should just be plugged into an LLM as an encoder, a sort of peripheral that translates images into tokens so the language model can do the "real" thinking. That works for a lot of practical tasks like captioning, VQA, and document understanding, but in a way it's still asking vision to serve language. If you care about spatial intelligence, about embodied agents, about building a world model, then vision has to be a first-class citizen. The representation has to be learned from the visual world itself, and maybe language becomes an interface on top of it rather than the foundation underneath.

So, in short: LLMs are great at manipulating abstractions, and vision is about where those abstractions come from in the first place. I think the next big step is figuring out how to learn those abstractions directly from sensory experience, and that's still very much an open problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts LLMs’ symbolic abstractions with vision’s grounding and sensory-world problems, but does not say these belong to different markets.

r002.rationale: It describes vision’s signal as continuous and identifies the challenge of extracting structure from that raw sensory stream, including how things move and interact over time.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the clearest way to put it is that language is already a compressed representation of the world. When an LLM reads text, somebody has already done the hard work of deciding what matters, what to name, what to leave out. So language models are largely learning the structure of human thought as it's been written down. That's an enormous amount of knowledge, and the recipe is relatively clean: next-token prediction scales beautifully because the data is discrete, it's dense in meaning, and the objective aligns naturally with the data.

Vision is a different situation. The pixels come from the physical world, not from a human who has pre-filtered them. There's no "token" that comes for free. Most of the signal is redundant, a lot of it is irrelevant for any given task, and the useful parts are entangled with lighting, viewpoint, occlusion, and so on. So the problem vision has to solve first is representation: what should the basic unit be, what should be invariant, what should be preserved. Language gets that from humans; vision has to discover it.

That's why I think the questions are actually quite different. For LLMs, the questions right now are largely about reasoning, alignment, and what emerges at scale. For vision, we're still asking foundational questions: how do you learn from raw sensory data without labels, how do you get a model to understand 3D structure, physics, how objects move and interact. These are things a child learns before language. If you look at it that way, LLMs are solving the "cultural knowledge" problem, and vision has to solve the "perception and grounding" problem, which is in some sense older and lower-level.

And the two need each other. An LLM without perception can talk about the world but can't see it. A vision model without language has a hard time connecting what it sees to the abstractions humans care about. So I don't see them as competing. I see vision as the part that connects intelligence back to the physical world, and that's the part we haven't really cracked yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes different problem types for LLMs and vision, but does not characterize them as belonging to fundamentally different markets.

r002.rationale: It mentions 3D structure, physics, and how objects move and interact, but does not identify continuity as a defining challenge.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is how much of the problem has already been expressed in language. Language is an incredibly useful representation, but it’s also a compressed representation of the world. When we describe something, we’ve already selected the objects, the relationships, and the details we think matter. LLMs are very good at working with that representation—connecting concepts, drawing on knowledge, and following instructions.

With vision, you often have to discover that structure in the first place. You start with pixels. What is an object? Which parts belong together? How does something move, and what stays the same when your viewpoint changes? A lot of that information is difficult to capture precisely in words.

For example, describing a room and moving through that room are different problems. You can say, ‘There’s a chair next to the table,’ but that doesn’t tell you the exact geometry, whether you can fit through the gap, or what will happen if you push the chair. Those questions require a more detailed connection to the physical world.

So I wouldn’t draw the boundary simply as text versus images. The question is whether language gives you enough information to solve the task. If it does, an LLM can be extremely powerful. If the task depends on spatial detail, motion, or physical interaction that language leaves out, then perception has substantial work to do. Connecting those capabilities is exciting, but we shouldn’t assume that being able to talk about the world is the same as understanding everything needed to act in it.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes language-based reasoning from vision’s work with pixels and physical detail, but it does not argue that they belong to fundamentally different markets.

r002.rationale: It mentions motion and what stays the same across viewpoints, but does not identify continuity as a defining challenge vision must handle.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction starts with the representation. With language, a lot of the world has already been abstracted for you. When we describe something in words, we’ve selected what matters and organized it into concepts. That makes language a very powerful space for learning, but it also means some of the work has happened before the model sees the input.

Vision has to deal with what comes before that abstraction. You get pixels, and you have to figure out what’s there, how things relate, what’s changing, and which details matter for the task. If you’re trying to manipulate an object, for example, knowing its name isn’t enough. You need to understand its geometry, where it is, and what might happen when you touch it.

So I wouldn’t draw the boundary simply as text versus images. It’s more about the kind of understanding the problem requires. Some visual questions can be answered once you translate the image into a description. Others depend on spatial detail, motion, or interaction that a description may leave out. Language models give us a powerful interface and a lot of useful knowledge, but there’s still a substantial problem in learning representations grounded in the visual world.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts language and vision by representation and the kind of understanding required, but does not argue that they belong to fundamentally different markets.

r002.rationale: It mentions change and motion as visual concerns, but does not identify continuity as a defining challenge.
